1.Nf3 Nf6 2.c4 g6.name: English Opening: Anglo-Indian Defence, King's Indian Formation
1.Nf3 Nf6 2.c4 g6.background: Until the mid-1930s the King's Indian Defence was generally regarded as highly suspect, but the analysis and play of three Soviet players in particular, Alexander Konstantinopolsky, Isaac Boleslavsky and David Bronstein, helped to make it much more respected and popular.

1.Nf3 Nf6 2.c4 g6 3.g3.strategy: Fianchettoes the king's bishop against Black's own fianchetto set-up. The bishop eyes the long diagonal and the queenside, White keeps the d-pawn flexible, and the game is a strategic, manoeuvring one in which neither side has committed to a pawn centre yet.

1.Nf3 Nf6 2.c4 g6 3.b4.strategy: A wing pawn thrust that grabs queenside space and prepares a bishop on the long diagonal. But the advanced pawn has no pawn support and can be attacked from the flank, and it loosens the c3 square. Offbeat and playable, not a way to fight for an advantage.
1.Nf3 Nf6 2.c4 g6 3.b4.name: English Orangutan

1.Nf3 Nf6 2.c4 g6 3.g3 Bg7.strategy: Completes Black's own fianchetto and puts the bishop on the long diagonal, aimed at White's queenside once the knight on f6 moves. Black keeps every pawn set-up open and can castle next, so the choice between challenging the centre at once and building a compact position stays with Black.

1.Nf3 Nf6 2.c4 g6 3.g3 d5.strategy: Strikes at c4 at once, before White has built a pawn centre. If White takes, Black's knight recaptures on an active central square and the bishop on g7 will bear on the long diagonal. A direct, respectable way to fight for equality.
1.Nf3 Nf6 2.c4 g6 3.g3 d5.name: English Opening: Anglo-Indian Defence, Grünfeld Formation

1.Nf3 Nf6 2.c4 g6 3.g3 b6.strategy: Prepares the second fianchetto, with the bishop contesting the long diagonal and the e4 square. Black controls the centre from a distance rather than occupying it. Sound and flexible, but it delays the king's bishop and leaves the centre to White for now.

1.Nf3 Nf6 2.c4 g6 3.g3 c6.strategy: Prepares to support a later central pawn thrust and keeps the queen's bishop free. It is solid but slow: a pawn move that develops no piece, so White gets time to build up and Black has to be patient before the centre can be challenged.
1.Nf3 Nf6 2.c4 g6 3.g3 c6.name: English Opening: Anglo-Indian Defence, Slav Formation

1.Nf3 Nf6 2.c4 g6 3.g3 b6 4.Bg2.strategy: Develops the bishop on the long diagonal and prepares castling. Both sides now have a fianchetto plan, and the bishop on g2 presses on the centre and the long diagonal that Black's queen's bishop wants to occupy.

1.Nf3 Nf6 2.c4 g6 3.g3 b6 4.Bg2 Bb7.name: English Opening: Anglo-Indian Defence, King's Indian Formation, Double Fianchetto
1.Nf3 Nf6 2.c4 g6 3.g3 b6 4.Bg2 Bb7.strategy: Black develops the queen's bishop on the long diagonal and has the king's bishop still to place. The double fianchetto controls the centre from a distance and leaves the pawn structure flexible, and Black has to decide later where the central break comes.

1.Nf3 Nf6 2.c4 g6 3.g3 Bg7 4.Bg2.strategy: Completes the fianchetto: the bishop looks down the long diagonal and White can castle at once. Both sides now have the same king's-side set-up, and the fight is for the centre and the queenside rather than for development.

1.Nf3 Nf6 2.c4 g6 3.g3 Bg7 4.Bg2 O-O.strategy: Black castles and puts the king behind its fianchettoed bishop. It also frees a rook and keeps the choice of central plan open. Nothing is committed in the centre yet, so the game stays flexible for both sides.

1.Nf3 Nf6 2.c4 g6 3.g3 Bg7 4.Bg2 O-O 5.O.strategy: White follows suit and the two fianchetto set-ups are mirrored. Neither side has a pawn centre yet, so the next moves decide the character of the game: the side that takes space in the centre first sets the agenda.

Stakes a claim on d4 and takes queenside space, answering White's c-pawn with its own. A symmetrical set-up follows, in which Black has a solid position and no weaknesses, a good choice for a quiet middlegame.

Brings another piece into the fight for the centre: the knight eyes d5 and supports a later central advance. White keeps the pressure on the d5 square while every pawn structure remains possible, so Black has to be precise about what to allow.
Develops the knight to its best square, covering d4 and e5, so White cannot build a pawn centre cheaply. A slow, symmetrical manoeuvring game follows: solid equality for Black, with little to attack.
